# "Disaster is Rarely as Pervasive as it Seems from Recorded Accounts" — Barbara Tuchman: A Discussion

## Introduction

In the introduction to her 1978 book *A Distant Mirror*, Tuchman identified a historical phenomenon she termed "Tuchman's Law." Its essence is both simple and profound: disaster is rarely as pervasive as it seems from recorded accounts. The fact of being on the record makes it appear continuous and ubiquitous, whereas it is more likely to have been sporadic both in time and place. Besides, persistence of the normal is usually greater than the effect of the disturbance.

Tuchman extended this observation into a formal principle: "The fact of being reported multiplies the apparent extent of any deplorable development by five- to tenfold."

This is a rich and challenging claim. It invites us to scrutinize how history is recorded, who records it, and what structural biases shape the archive we inherit. It is a claim that is substantially — though not unconditionally — correct, and it has profound implications for how we read the past, and indeed the present.

---

## I. The Argument in Context: *A Distant Mirror* and the Fourteenth Century

Tuchman formulated her law while writing about the calamitous fourteenth century — an age of the Black Death, the Hundred Years' War, peasant revolts, schisms in the Church, and famine. It would be easy, reading the chronicles, to imagine medieval Europe as a landscape of unrelieved horror. Yet Tuchman urges caution.

There were many things that apparently didn't change much after the Black Death. The basic structure of medieval society and politics remained remarkably stable, and changes in literature, art, architecture and religion are subtle at best. It is possible that the plague killed huge numbers of people but didn't change structural elements of medieval society dramatically.

Recent bioarchaeological research supports this view powerfully. Although the epidemic killed millions, no dramatic changes in skeletal indicators of health and lifestyle are directly ascribable to the epidemic. Most indicators either remained stable or changed in response to other known historical trends. Traumatic though the plague was, it did not transform medieval people's health and lifeways radically.

This is precisely Tuchman's point: the catastrophe was real, but so was the everyday continuity of human life that the records largely ignore.

---

## II. The Problem of the Record: Why Disasters Are Over-Represented

### A. The Intrinsic Bias of Documentation

The most powerful support for Tuchman's Law lies in how historical records are created. Events that are extraordinary — battles, plagues, famines, political collapses — are precisely the events that contemporaries feel compelled to write down. The mundane, the routine, the ordinary day of the peasant, the merchant, the mother, the child, goes largely unrecorded. This creates a profound structural imbalance in the archive.

Survivorship bias is the tendency to focus solely on surviving entities or successful outcomes, while neglecting those that did not survive or were not successful. It arises from factors such as data availability, selection bias, and reporting biases, leading to distorted perceptions of reality.

In historical terms, survivorship bias is a statistical error that results from concentrating on entities that passed a selection process while overlooking those that did not, leading to incorrect conclusions because of incomplete data.

The very documents that survive — chronicles, royal decrees, ecclesiastical records, lamentation poetry — are the products of literate, institutional, often elite actors whose perception of events was coloured by their position and purpose.

### B. The Chronicler's Perspective

Medieval chroniclers are among the most important sources for calamitous events, yet they were far from neutral observers. Medieval chroniclers occupied a position of perceived authority that made their work particularly powerful as a vehicle for political narrative. They were often clerics, court affiliates, or individuals dependent on noble patronage, embedded within the very power structures they described. Their writings were not detached records of events but interpretive constructions shaped by loyalty, obligation, and audience expectation.

Consequently, chroniclers selected events with intention. What they chose to record, emphasize, or omit reflected political priorities rather than comprehensive documentation. Victories received detailed treatment, defeats were abbreviated or reframed, and controversial episodes were softened or displaced.

Furthermore, the figures themselves were often unreliable. High casualty figures in medieval chronicles are certainly exaggerations, as it seems doubtful the chronicler would have had access to any accurate figures. Such high figures were merely used by medieval writers to illustrate that a very high number had died.

Using chronicles as historical sources requires readers to recognise that the writers often recorded events from a particular point of view. Chroniclers recording battles often got important names correct, but when one compares various battle records, one finds a "troubling sameness."

### C. The Elite Perspective and Invisible Majorities

A further dimension of recording bias is class and gender. Until relatively recently, mainstream Western historical narratives focused on political and military history, while cultural or social history was written mostly from the perspective of the elites. Consequently, what was in fact the experience of a selected few was typically presented as the illustrative experience of the entire society.

This means that when a chronicler describes a disaster — a plague, a war, a famine — he describes it as experienced by those closest to power. The vast peasant majority, whose daily life may have been disrupted far less dramatically (or, conversely, far more terribly in ways left unrecorded), is largely absent. Large, successful organisations such as the Women's Institute, which were well organised and still have accessible archives, are studied more than smaller charitable organisations, even though these may have done a great deal of work. The same principle extends to entire social classes: the well-documented suffer more historiographical attention than the undocumented.

---

## III. Tuchman's Law in the Modern World

Tuchman was also alert to the contemporary relevance of her observation. After absorbing the news of today, one expects to face a world consisting entirely of strikes, crimes, power failures, broken water mains, stalled trains, school shutdowns, muggers, drug addicts, neo-Nazis, and rapists. The fact is that one can come home in the evening — on a lucky day — without having encountered more than one or two of these phenomena.

Tuchman's Law has been defined as a psychological principle of "perceptual readiness" or "subjective probability" — a useful guide to how we misunderstand the world's dangers, fuelled by television and other media where random but rare acts of violence seem more prevalent than the higher rates of harm that stem from financial fraud and corporate or government decisions.

The mechanism is the same whether the "record" is a medieval chronicle or a twenty-four-hour news cycle: extraordinary, negative events are over-represented relative to the unremarkable continuity of normal life.

---

## IV. Where Tuchman's Law Has Limits: When Disaster Really Is Pervasive

### A. Some Disasters Are Not Exaggerated

Tuchman's Law is presented as a corrective against over-reading catastrophe, but it must not become an excuse for under-reading it. Some disasters are every bit as pervasive as the record suggests — or more so.
